| **Names** | **9** | **15** | **+6** |

The rest of this report sets out our latest findings, where they differ from current market consensus, and why they led us to add new names to the basket.

## Section 1: Identity: the layer we like most

**Cybersecurity needs a new definition.** The old job was keeping outsiders out. Today companies authorise software to act on their behalf, so risk also starts inside, with logins and permissions the company granted itself.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig1.png" alt="Two of the four risks now start inside the company" />

Risks 1 and 2 are the familiar hacker story. Risks 3 and 4 are new and sit inside the company. All four end at the same checkpoint: a valid login with permissions. That checkpoint is the identity layer.

**Where the money sits today.** Half of 2026 enterprise security product spend (about $145B, Gartner) sits in three layers:

| Layer | 2026 spend | Share | Main names |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Network and edge | about $30B | 21% | FTNT, PANW, ZS, NET |
| **Identity** | **about $23B** | **16%** | **SAIL, PANW, CRWD, MSFT** |
| Endpoint | about $21B | 14% | CRWD, MSFT |
| Top three | about $74B | 51% |  |

Identity is the second-largest pool today, behind network. We favour it because it has the strongest breach evidence of any layer and the clearest new demand driver.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig2.png" alt="Sources: Gartner information security forecast (identity and access management, 2026), Okta annual reports (fiscal years end January), SailPoint earnings releases (Q4 FY26, Q2 FY27), via Quartr." />

*Sources: Gartner information security forecast (identity and access management, 2026), Okta annual reports (fiscal years end January), SailPoint earnings releases (Q4 FY26, Q2 FY27), via Quartr.*

**What the incident data says.** The 2026 incident datasets all point to identity:

- Identity played a material role in about 90% of Unit 42's 750+ cases, and 65% of initial access was identity-based.
- Credential abuse appears in 39% of breaches in Verizon's DBIR. 73% of ransomware victims had stolen credentials for sale beforehand, half of them within 95 days of the attack.
- 99% of 680,000+ cloud identities held excessive permissions (Unit 42).
- Attacks are moving from email to phone calls and agents. A vishing call and a hijacked agent end in the same place: a valid login (DBIR, CrowdStrike).

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig3.png" alt="Cloudflare: a growing share of web traffic is non-human" />

*Source: Cloudflare.*

**Why the layer grows with AI agents.**

- Machine identities (service accounts, API keys, agents) already outnumber people by roughly 80 to 100 to 1, and most are ungoverned.
- SailPoint's October survey: 79% of organisations run AI agents in production, but only 2% have identity tools built to govern them.
- If pricing moves from per employee to per identity, every agent becomes billable. SailPoint has introduced pricing it says will "scale in lockstep" with agent growth.
- Platforms are buying in: PANW-CyberArk (about $25B), CRWD-SGNL ($740M) and CSCO-Astrix all closed within about a year. Those prices set a floor for independent assets.

**The caveat.** The demand has not yet reached reported revenue: SAIL grows about 17% and OKTA about 11%.

**Why we expect identity to outgrow its share.** Identity is only the second-largest pool today, but the two charts below show why we expect its spend to accelerate. Companies are adopting AI agents quickly: downloads of the toolkit that connects agents to company systems rose about 7x in a year.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig4.png" alt="Agent adoption: MCP SDK downloads up about 7x in a year" />

*Source: npm monthly downloads. Monthly data to Sep 2026. MCP launched Nov 2024.*

Attackers are following, and the monthly count of malicious packages imitating AI tools is up about 6x. Every agent needs a login and permissions, and every stolen agent credential is a new way in. We therefore expect identity spend to grow faster than Gartner's 12% forecast, and faster than most other layers, as agents multiply.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig5.png" alt="Attacks on agents: malicious packages imitating AI tools" />

*Source: OSV malicious-package records, matched by package name. Data to Oct 24, 2026.*

Every one of these malicious packages has to pass through a company's software store before it can do harm. JFrog (FROG) runs that store for 83% of the Fortune 100, and its Curation tool blocks malicious packages and AI models before developers or agents can pull them in. It now also manages registries for the tools agents connect to (MCP servers). We cover FROG in more detail in Section 3.

**Why SAIL over OKTA.** The two listed pure plays in identity are Okta (OKTA) and SailPoint (SAIL). We prefer SAIL for three reasons:

- **Better growth for the price.** The two trade at similar multiples (about 12x forward sales for OKTA, 10x for SAIL), but SAIL's ARR is growing about 25% against OKTA's 11%. Adjusted for growth, OKTA is the more expensive stock.
- **A harder moat.** OKTA's core product is login: single sign-on and multi-factor authentication. That is the part of identity that bundlers find easiest to copy, led by Microsoft's Entra, which comes inside M365. SAIL sells governance: deciding who and what should have access, reviewing it and removing it. That needs deep connections into thousands of old and new applications, and the audit trail regulators rely on, so it is much harder to replace.
- **Growth that tracks agent numbers.** Every new agent, service account and API key needs to be governed, so SAIL's opportunity grows with the number of identities, not just the number of employees. SAIL has already moved to pricing it says will "scale in lockstep" with agent growth. OKTA's login business does not scale one-for-one with agents, because many agents reuse existing logins and tokens.

For more detail, see the identity layer in our [September primer](/research/cybersecurity-theme-primer/).

**A smaller name for consideration: Mitek (MITK).** Mitek fits the same identity trend. It trades more thinly than the names above and will be more volatile, but on valuation it is more attractive than many better-known peers, at about 4x sales and a market value of about $0.8B. We add it to the basket at a small weight.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig6.png" alt="AI is making fraud harder to spot" />

*Source: Mitek.*

Mitek is really two companies wearing one trench coat:

- **Check verification (about 47% of revenue).** It checks cheques deposited by phone. It is not exciting, but it generates steady, profitable revenue in a business unlikely to disappear in the next five years.
- **Fraud and identity (about 53%, up from 44% in 2024).** This is the part that matters for our thesis. Mitek helps banks and other high-assurance businesses confirm that a customer is real and authorised, using document checks, facial biometrics, liveness detection (proving a live person, not a photo or deepfake) and behavioural and device signals. Management expects this segment to grow about 19% in fiscal 2026, to $105 to $109M, with its SaaS revenue growing faster still.

**The main risk** is Microsoft bundling Entra identity into M365, which we cover in Section 5. We believe our basket exposure (MITK, SAIL, PANW, CRWD and MSFT) hedges this risk. This is also why we prefer to play the theme through a basket rather than any single stock: each name carries idiosyncratic risks that are not relevant to the theme.

## Section 2: Network and edge: the largest pool, with two ways to win

Network and edge security is the largest layer of 2026 enterprise security spend, at about $30B (21% of the total, see the table above). Gartner puts network security equipment at $27.2B, growing 15%, of which firewalls are $19.7B. Zero-trust network access, the cloud alternative to the VPN, is smaller at $3.0B but growing faster at 23%. The money is moving in two directions at once, and the four names we track cover both.

**1. Firewalls remain essential, and their weakness is driving demand.** Every company still needs a box where its network meets the internet: the firewall and VPN. That box is now the most attacked security product.

- Exploiting software flaws is now the number-one way into a company (31% of breaches, Verizon DBIR), mostly through edge devices. 40% of China-linked exploitation targeted them (CrowdStrike).
- These appliances are closed systems, so endpoint tools like CrowdStrike cannot run on them. In one case a China-linked group entered through a VPN box and stayed hidden for 22 months, because no security software was watching (CrowdStrike, "Warp Panda").
- 44% of the network access sold by initial access brokers is VPN access (DBIR).

The market response has been to upgrade, not to leave. Fortinet's product revenue grew 52% in Q2 2026. AI adds a second driver: AI workloads create heavy traffic inside the data centre, between GPU servers, agents and databases. Sending that traffic out to a cloud service to be checked is slow and costly, so it still needs fast physical firewalls on site. Fortinet's custom chips are built for this.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig7.png" alt="Fortinet product revenue and SASE ARR" />

**2. Security is moving to the cloud, and SASE is taking share.** Users, applications and now AI agents sit outside the office network, so a box at the office perimeter protects less each year. Cloud-delivered security, known as SASE (secure access service edge) or SSE (security service edge, the same thing without the networking part), replaces it with a broker in the vendor's cloud:

- **Per-application access:** a VPN lets a user onto the whole network once logged in. SASE connects each user, or agent, to one approved app at a time, so a stolen login reaches far less.
- **Nothing to attack at the edge:** there is no internet-facing box, and the vendor patches its own cloud centrally, rather than waiting for each customer to patch.
- **Agent traffic control:** agents call outside tools and data sources constantly. A cloud broker can inspect and block that traffic in the path, wherever the agent runs.

This shows in the numbers. Zscaler's branch and cloud products have grown over 60% a year for eight quarters, and Palo Alto's SASE business grows about 40%, faster than the market.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig8.png" alt="Zscaler ARR history" />

**3. How the four names split the opportunity**

|  | Position | Latest growth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FTNT | Firewall hardware leader, own chips, adding cloud SASE | Product revenue +52%, SASE ARR +18% |
| PANW | Both models: firewalls plus Prisma Access, sold as a platform | SASE ARR about +40% (about $1.6B) |
| ZS | Largest cloud-native SASE pure play | ARR $3.8B, +25% (about +20% organic) |
| NTSK | Cloud-native challenger, strongest in data and SaaS control | ARR $0.9B, +27% |

FTNT and PANW win if customers want one vendor for network and security, and as data centres add firewalls for AI traffic. ZS and NTSK win if security moves fully to the cloud and is bought separately from the network. Tracking all four means we do not need to call which model wins. NTSK has not yet reached the conviction level we want for the basket, so we hold FTNT, PANW and ZS and keep watching Netskope.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig9.png" alt="SASE ARR: ZS, PANW, FTNT and NTSK" />

**Risks**

- FTNT: Part of Fortinet's product growth came from one-off price increases, but clearly management understands that and FTNT is pushing on the growth of their SASE revenue.
- PANW: Palo Alto gave no SASE ARR figure for its latest quarter (it only described growth qualitatively on the call).
- NTSK: Netskope's growth is slowing, from 34% to 27%, and its net retention fell from 118% to 114%. That is a familiar pattern in this sector. As smaller specialists slow, they tend to become acquisition targets for platforms that can sell their product into a much larger customer base: Palo Alto bought CyberArk, Cisco bought Splunk and CrowdStrike bought SGNL. If Netskope's growth keeps fading, a sale to a platform such as Palo Alto becomes a realistic outcome.

## Section 3: The bottleneck is fixing, not finding

**Finding flaws is becoming cheap.** Frontier AI models are now among the most productive vulnerability researchers in the world: Anthropic's Mythos, OpenAI's Codex Security and Google's Big Sleep find serious bugs at internet scale. Even Qualys concedes that "traditional scanning and detection have become table stakes". Scanning is the part of security most easily vibe-coded away.

**Fixing them is not.** **Companies fully fix only 26% of known-exploited vulnerabilities, and the median time to fix rose to 43 days from 32 (Verizon DBIR)**. AI is widening the gap: of about 530 serious bugs Mythos reported to open-source maintainers, only 75 were patched. Patching at scale needs software on every machine, change control, staged rollout and the ability to roll back, none of which a model can do on its own.

**The race starts at disclosure.** When a vulnerability is announced, defenders and attackers learn about it at the same moment. Attackers know a typical company takes weeks to patch, so the alert itself becomes their starting gun. Increasingly they do not even wait: Mandiant estimates attackers now exploit flaws about 7 days before they are disclosed.

**PHP2Shell showed the answer.** In October, two critical flaws in PHP, the software behind a large share of websites, let attackers take over unpatched servers.

**The fallout was global, and it hit within a day.** On Oct 21 and 22, governments and companies pulled their own websites offline rather than risk an attack (Reuters):

- **Europe's governments went dark.** Germany's federal IT provider, France's Interior Ministry (prefecture websites), Belgium's foreign ministry, the Czech government and Finland's state IT centre, which shut all of the government's public web services.
- **The Netherlands shut down almost everything public-facing.** Following the national cyber centre's lead, the Port of Rotterdam, the government portal Overheid.nl, the national football association, the five largest political parties and numerous hospitals all took their websites offline.
- **Japan's state and its largest companies suspended services.** The National Tax Agency took its service down, and the Ministry of Finance and the Meteorological Agency partially suspended theirs. Nomura, MUFG, ANA and East Japan Railway suspended some online services as emergency measures.
- **Household names went offline.** The Wikimedia Foundation (Wikipedia) took down a number of systems and said all its systems using PHP were affected. The Internet Archive took its portal offline, the BBC took down some web portals, and Orange suspended websites and apps across several subsidiaries.
- **It reached North America and local government too.** Canada warned that some government websites might be unavailable, and UK councils, including the City of Edinburgh, took services down.

Most of these shutdowns were precautions, not responses to confirmed breaches. That is the point: when the patch is days away, organisations without a shield in front of their websites have only one option, which is to switch them off.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig10.png" alt="Exploit and patch timeline, October 2026" />

Unit 42 counted 22.6 million potentially vulnerable instances. Exploit attempts were seen on Oct 17, four days before the patch was released on Oct 21. Cloudflare (NET) had blocking rules live in its web application firewall (WAF) at 03:02 UTC on Oct 21. This is virtual patching: the vendor blocks the attack in the traffic path, which buys customers time to apply the real fix. We believe NET and FSLY will both do well as WAF providers.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig11.png" alt="Cloudflare network overview" />

*Source: Cloudflare investor materials.*

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig12.png" alt="Cloudflare: connect, protect and build AI" />

*Source: Cloudflare investor materials.*

**Where JFrog (FROG) fits: shipping the fix.** If fixing is the bottleneck, someone has to deliver the fix safely. JFrog runs the system that stores, scans and distributes every piece of software a company builds or downloads, from source code out to the cloud, its own data centres and edge devices such as cars and factory machines. It is a single platform that combines developer operations, security and release management, used by 83% of the Fortune 100.

AI makes this more valuable, not less. Even if AI can write an entire banking stack or update an airline's databases across thousands of devices, these systems have near-zero tolerance for faults, and lives can depend on them. So engineering teams are consolidating onto one platform that can trace, check and roll back every release, rather than stitching together tools. JFrog benefits from this platform shift because it offers reference designs and services that each company can shape to its own teams.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig13.png" alt="The JFrog software supply chain platform" />

*Source: JFrog.*

The numbers support it. In Q2 2026 revenue grew 29% to $164M, cloud revenue grew 53%, and customers spending over $1M a year rose to 97 from 61. Security is now the growth engine: 80% of new $1M+ customers bought JFrog's security products, and gross retention is 97%.

**B****a****s****k****et**** ****to ****ex****pre****ss this ****finding****:**

| Role | Names | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fix | QLYS | The only listed security vendor with a real patching business |
| Ship the fix | FROG | Stores, scans and rolls out every software release to cloud, on-prem and edge devices |
| Shield | NET, FFIV (AKAM, FSLY tracked, not held) | Sit in front of websites and block attack traffic before it reaches unpatched servers |
| Avoid | TENB, RPD | Revenue depends on finding flaws, the part AI is commoditising |

**Why we like QLYS.** The market groups Qualys with the vulnerability scanners and has de-rated it with them. But patching already makes up about 9% of its bookings over the past year and 16% of new bookings. That share is still small, but it is growing, and it sits in the bottleneck. QLYS is in our new basket.

**The proof in Qualys's numbers.** Qualys does not report revenue by product, but since early 2026 it has disclosed patch management's share of bookings on every call. Patching rose from 7% of bookings in 2024 to 8% in 2025 and 9% in the 12 months to June 2026, and it has held at about 16% of new bookings throughout. Applied to revenue, that puts patching at roughly $63M a year, growing about 26% in 2025 against about 9% for the rest of the business.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig14.png" alt="Sources: Qualys earnings calls (Q4 2025, Q1 and Q2 2026) for patch management&#x27;s share of bookings, and Qualys revenue via Quartr. Patching revenue is our estimate." />

*Sources: Qualys earnings calls (Q4 2025, Q1 and Q2 2026) for patch management's share of bookings, and Qualys revenue via Quartr. Patching revenue is our estimate.*

Patching is still a small business, but it is the fastest-growing part of Qualys and it accounts for about a sixth of all new business. Among listed vulnerability-management vendors, Qualys is the only one with a meaningful patching product. Tenable and Rapid7 have essentially none. Larger patching businesses do exist, but they sit inside much bigger companies (Microsoft Intune, ServiceNow) or are private (Tanium, NinjaOne).

**Why we avoid TENB and RPD.** Tenable grows about 9%, with essentially no patching revenue. Rapid7 has the same exposure to detection, and its revenue is already shrinking.

On the shield side, Cloudflare and F5 are in our basket. Akamai and Fastly (FSLY) offer the same WAF protection, but we leave them out of the basket. Fastly is smaller with a higher beta, so we use Cloudflare to represent the WAF theme. Akamai is explained below.

**Why not Akamai.** Akamai has a real security business, but the stock is increasingly a bet on building cloud infrastructure. **It expects capital spending of about 40% of revenue in 2026, and its legacy content-delivery business is shrinking by mid-single digits.** Its new $11.6 billion multi-year agreement with Anthropic is for computing capacity, not security. The deal adds no revenue in 2026, needs about 100 megawatts of new capacity to deliver, and gives Anthropic warrants for up to 5% of Akamai's shares. Headlines like this can move a low-quality stock sharply, but that is beta from a capital-heavy business, not the quality we invest in. Cloudflare and F5 give us the same shield exposure with stronger fundamentals.

## Section 4: The hidden layer is people

Section 3 showed that fixing is the bottleneck. Part of the reason is simple: there are not enough skilled people to do the work. So we also look at the market horizontally, by who is paid, not just by which layer is protected.

**Who spends, and on what.** Gartner puts worldwide security spending at $247.5B in 2026. Consumers are a rounding error. More than 95% is spent by companies, led by the Fortune 500 and governments, and** almost 40% of that goes not to software but to people: consultants, integrators and outsourced monitoring.**

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig15.png" alt="Source: Gartner information security forecast, 2026 ($247.5B total)." />

*Source: Gartner information security forecast, 2026 ($247.5B total).*

**The labour shortage is real and getting worse.** In ISC2's 2025 workforce study of more than 16,000 security professionals:

- 95% of teams reported at least one skills gap, and 59% called their gaps critical or significant, up from 44% a year earlier.
- 88% had at least one security incident or operational problem they linked to a skills shortage.
- 36% faced budget cuts and 24% had layoffs, while 72% agreed that cutting security staff significantly raises the risk of a breach.
- The most-needed skills are AI (41%) and cloud security (36%), which are exactly what agent rollouts require.

Attackers do not wait for hiring. The average intruder spreads from the first machine to others in 29 minutes (CrowdStrike), and few companies can staff a security operations centre around the clock. That gap is what the $95B services pool pays for.

**Where the services money goes.** It splits into two very different businesses:

- **Ongoing monitoring** (managed detection and response) is moving to the security platforms, because their AI agents now do much of the triage analysts used to do. This benefits CRWD, PANW and MSFT. CrowdStrike Falcon Complete, Palo Alto's Unit 42 and Microsoft Defender Experts all sell it, and only large platforms can afford to run this labour-intensive, lower-margin service.
- **One-off projects** stay with the consultants: designing security programmes, deploying identity and agent controls across thousands of applications, and meeting regulatory deadlines. Every company rolling out AI agents needs this work done once, and quickly.

**Our services names**** ****\[****n****ew p****i****ck\]**

- **Accenture (ACN):** the largest IT consultancy in the world, with a dedicated security practice. It wins enterprise-wide AI and security transformation projects for commercial clients, and reported record bookings in its latest quarter.
- **SAIC (tracked, not held):** a US government IT contractor that modernises federal agency systems, including cloud migration and cyber defence.
- **CACI:** a US national-security contractor focused on defence and intelligence agencies, including cyber operations and electronic warfare.

CACI gives us mandated government cyber spending, which does not depend on corporate IT budgets. SAIC offers similar exposure, but we track it rather than hold it. ACN and CACI are small weights, because neither reports security revenue separately and AI also threatens part of their billable-hours model.

**The numbers behind the labour side.**

- **Accenture's security practice is now a $10B business.** Accenture does not report security as a segment, but on its Q3 FY26 call it said its security services grew from about $700M in FY16 to $10B in FY25. That is about 35% growth a year by Accenture's own count, about four times the group's, and security has gone from 2% to about 14% of revenue. It is now buying security software too: Dragos, runZero and NetRise for industrial (OT) security, part of about $9B of acquisitions planned this fiscal year.

  <img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig16.png" alt="Sources: Accenture Q3 FY26 earnings call (security services about $700M in FY16 and $10B in FY25), Accenture annual revenue via Quartr." />

*Sources: Accenture Q3 FY26 earnings call (security services about $700M in FY16 and $10B in FY25), Accenture annual revenue via Quartr.*
- **CACI keeps growing.** CACI does not break out cyber revenue, but group revenue rose 11% to $9.6B in its fiscal year to June 2026, and about 58% since FY21. SAIC also does not report cyber separately.
- **Hiring is picking up again.** US employers posted 514,359 cybersecurity job listings in the 12 months to April 2025 (the latest CyberSeek data), up about 57,000 or 12% on the prior year (CyberSeek, CompTIA and NIST). There are only 74 available workers for every 100 openings.

  <img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig17.png" alt="Source: CyberSeek (CompTIA and NIST), June 2025 release covering May 2024 to April 2025." />

*Source: CyberSeek (CompTIA and NIST), June 2025 release covering May 2024 to April 2025.*

## Section 5: Who is the real threat?

The market's biggest fear this year has been the frontier labs. Anthropic's Mythos and Claude Code Security, and OpenAI's Codex Security, showed that AI can now find software flaws at internet scale, and security stocks were repriced for AI disruption. CrowdStrike fell about 36% from its November 2025 high to around $90 in March (split-adjusted), before recovering to $258.

**We think the fear is aimed at the wrong target. The labs replace work that is about *finding* and *labour*. The bundlers, meaning Microsoft and the hyperscalers that add security to products customers already pay for, threaten almost every layer. **We went back through each layer of our framework and asked two questions: can a frontier lab build this, and can a bundler give it away?

| Layer | Labs replace it? | Bundlers squeeze it? | Relevant tickers (basket) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Finding flaws (scanning) | Yes | Yes (Microsoft Defender) | QLYS (TENB, RPD not held) |
| Code security | Yes | Yes (GitHub Copilot Autofix) | FROG, MSFT (GitHub) |
| Agent runtime guardrails | Yes | Yes (lab and hyperscaler guardrails) | None pure-play. PANW, ZS, NET, CRWD add it as a feature |
| Security services | Yes (AI analysts) | Yes (platform-run monitoring) | ACN, CACI |
| Identity | No | Yes (Microsoft Entra in M365) | SAIL, MITK |
| Endpoint and detection | No | Yes (Defender in Microsoft E5) | CRWD |
| Cloud and data security | Partly | Yes (Purview, native cloud tools, Wiz in Google) | CRWD, PANW, ZS |
| Observability | No | Yes (native cloud monitoring) | DDOG |
| Network and edge | No | Partly (platform SASE bundles) | FTNT, PANW, ZS, NET, FFIV |
| Supply chain | Partly | Partly (GitHub) | FROG |
| Recovery | No | Partly (native cloud backup) | RBRK |
| Fixing and virtual patching | No | Partly (Microsoft patches its own estate) | QLYS (patching), NET, FFIV (WAF virtual patching) |
| **Total** | **4 yes, 2 partly** | **8 yes, 4 partly** |  |

**What the table shows.** Labs threaten four layers, and those are exactly the ones we avoid or underweight: detection-led scanners (TENB, RPD), code scanners and labour-heavy services. Bundlers press on every layer. The risk is not that a lab rebuilds CrowdStrike. It is that a CFO asks why the company pays for CrowdStrike when Defender is already in its Microsoft licence.

**How our basket handles it.** We hold the biggest bundlers directly. MSFT is the largest security vendor in the world, and PANW and CRWD are the two platforms with the breadth to consolidate rather than be consolidated. For the specialists (SAIL, ZS, FROG, DDOG, RBRK), we look for one of four things the bundlers cannot easily copy: a position in the traffic path, a sensor on the device, a system of record, or the authority to act. And we size them as satellites, not core positions.

## Section 6: Are we in bubble territory?

Cybersecurity stocks are not cheap, so the fair question is whether we are buying near a top. We looked at three past episodes when security and software stocks crashed.

**1. The 2000 dot-com peak, the closest parallel.** Security was a hot theme then too, and leaders traded at extreme multiples of sales: VeriSign at about 310x, Entrust at about 95x, Check Point at 60 to 70x. From 2000 to 2002 they fell 89 to 98%. VeriSign took 22 years to regain its peak, and Entrust never did.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig18.png" alt="Source: Interactive Brokers monthly closes, Sep 1999 to Dec 2002, split-adjusted (CHKP split dates from Check Point&#x27;s investor FAQ)." />

*Source: Interactive Brokers monthly closes, Sep 1999 to Dec 2002, split-adjusted (CHKP split dates from Check Point's investor FAQ).*

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig19.png" alt="Sources: 2000 from company 10-Ks and CFA Institute. Today: IBKR closes and company filings via Quartr, Oct 23, 2026." />

*Sources: 2000 from company 10-Ks and CFA Institute. Today: IBKR closes and company filings via Quartr, Oct 23, 2026.*

Today's basket is expensive in places, but it is nowhere near 1999. The median name trades at about 17x forward sales. Only CRWD (44x) and NET (40x) sit above Cisco's 39x at the 2000 peak, and the basket as a whole fits inside the bottom of the 2000 range.

**2. The 2021 to 2022 growth reset.** When interest rates rose, high-multiple software fell hard even though the businesses kept growing:

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig20.png" alt="Source: Interactive Brokers weekly closes, May 17, 2021 to May 16, 2022, split-adjusted." />

*Source: Interactive Brokers weekly closes, May 17, 2021 to May 16, 2022, split-adjusted.*

|  | Peak (Nov 2021) | Trough | Fall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NET | $222 | $37 (Nov 2022) | -83% |
| ZS | $376 | $85 (May 2023) | -77% |
| CRWD | $75 | $23 (Jan 2023) | -69% |

CRWD regained its peak in about two years and NET in about four. ZS is still about 32% below it.

**3. The 2026 AI-disruption scare.** When frontier labs showed they could find flaws at scale, the market sold first and asked questions later. From their November 2025 highs to their spring 2026 lows, CRWD fell about 36%, NET about 37% and ZS about 66%. All three have since rebounded sharply.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig21.png" alt="Source: Interactive Brokers weekly closes, May 5, 2025 to May 4, 2026, split-adjusted." />

*Source: Interactive Brokers weekly closes, May 5, 2025 to May 4, 2026, split-adjusted.*

**Each crash up close: six months either side of the peak.** The 2000 chart uses Cisco, Check Point, VeriSign and Microsoft, because CRWD, NET, ZS and PANW did not trade yet. It runs to Dec 2002, because the security names peaked months after the Nasdaq and crashed later. All three charts share the same log scale, so the moves can be compared directly.

**Our read.** This is not 1999. Valuations are high for a few leaders, not across the sector, and today's companies have real revenue, cash flow and recurring contracts that the 2000 names lacked. But the last two episodes show that 40 to 80% drawdowns happen even without a bubble, from rate shocks or disruption fears. That is why we hold a basket rather than single names, keep the most expensive stocks (CRWD, NET) at smaller weights, and add on sell-offs rather than chase strength.

*CRWD prices are split-adjusted. Highs and lows are monthly, from Interactive Brokers.*

## Section 7: Conclusion. The next 12 to 18 months

**We may be entering a Y2K-style cybersecurity spending cycle, but without Y2K's deadline. The opportunity is structural. The stock prices will still be cyclical.**

Two forces are pulling in opposite directions.

**Force 1: A Y2K scramble without a deadline.**

Before 2000, companies spent about $300 billion worldwide (about $100 billion in the US) preparing for a computer failure that might never happen. The spending was real because the risk was too large to ignore.

AI could create a similar dynamic. PHP2Shell is an early warning: AI-assisted security research is accelerating vulnerability discovery, while enterprises are only beginning to deploy autonomous agents.

Unlike Y2K, there is no midnight when the problem disappears. Every new agent, permission and data connection creates another potential security risk. Companies will need to continuously reassess their defences.

**Our thesis is that fear of the next incident will drive spending well before that incident actually happens.**

**Force 2: The valuation cycle.**

Strong cybersecurity demand does not guarantee strong stock performance.

We saw this in 2021–22, when rising rates crushed software valuations despite healthy revenue growth. We saw another correction in 2025–26, when fears of AI disrupting traditional software businesses weighed on security stocks.

The lesson is simple: we can be right about cybersecurity spending and still lose money if we buy at the wrong valuation.

### How the next 12–18 months could unfold

**Base case: Security spending accelerates, but stocks remain volatile.**

AI adoption expands the attack surface, and companies gradually increase security budgets. Revenue growth follows, but valuations fluctuate with interest rates and broader software sentiment. We would use significant market corrections to build positions selectively.

**Upside catalyst: A major AI-related cybersecurity scare.**

Imagine an AI-assisted attack or compromised enterprise agent causing widespread disruption at a major bank, exchange or hospital network.

SolarWinds and Colonial Pipeline demonstrated how high-profile incidents can accelerate government action and corporate security priorities. A comparable AI-related event could bring agent security to the top of boardroom agendas almost overnight.

<img src="/img/cyber-basket-update-oct26_fig22.png" alt="SolarWinds supply chain attack, 2020" />

This could trigger a faster spending cycle and a sector-wide re-rating, potentially lifting even lower-quality cybersecurity names.

**The risk: A valuation-driven correction, or a spending cycle that disappoints.**

Cybersecurity stocks have historically suffered severe drawdowns even when underlying demand remained healthy. Higher rates, stretched valuations or weaker-than-expected monetisation of AI security could trigger another correction.

And if the sector eventually enters a fear-driven buying frenzy, we should be prepared to take profits rather than assume the rally will continue indefinitely.

---

# Passport Control for Robots: SAIL vs OKTA

Date: 2026-10-09
Theme: Cybersecurity
URL: https://theme-radar.github.io/research/passport-control-for-robots/

*AI agents pay the identity registry, not the login. Two identity pure plays, one agent boom, and why the market is backing the wrong layer.*

## Key points (as of 9 October 2026)

- **Thesis.** AI agents make identity security bigger, but they pay the layer that governs identities, not the layer that logs them in. Governance is priced on the number of identities. Login is priced per employee, and Okta gives agent sign-on away free. Within listed identity, SailPoint (SAIL) owns the better-placed layer at the lower multiple.
- **SailPoint Inc (Nasdaq: SAIL), $20.02 at the 8 October 2026 close.** ARR $1.23bn, up 25%, and net revenue retention 113% in Q2 FY27 (quarter to 31 July 2026). EV about 8.8x FY27 guided revenue. View: the better way to own the agent identity theme, trading 13% below its $23 IPO price, with Thoma Bravo's 84.6% stake the main overhang. Next check: Q3 FY27 results on 8 December 2026, against guided net new ARR of $57-61m.
- **Okta Inc (Nasdaq: OKTA), $220.21 at the 8 October 2026 close.** Revenue $805m, up 11%, free cash flow margin 28% and net revenue retention 107% in Q2 FY27 (quarter to 31 July 2026). EV about 11.2x FY27 guided revenue. View: a strong cash business, but the shares are up 250% since 10 April 2026 on agent revenue that management calls "too small to show up in the numbers". Too expensive today. Next check: Q3 FY27 results on 1 December 2026.
- **Our own arithmetic.** About a third of SailPoint's yearly net new ARR lands in its fiscal Q4 (34% in FY26). Its contracted backlog due within 12 months (cRPO) has grown faster than ARR for two quarters: 27.2% against 25.4% in Q2 FY27.
- **Main risk.** SailPoint's new business is flat: $106m of net new ARR in H1 FY27 against $105m a year earlier. A Q4 FY27 figure below $85m would mean the agent pipeline is not converting. For Okta, charging for agent login volume would weaken the core argument of this piece.

## The thesis in six lines

1. Every AI agent is a new identity that needs to be registered, given permissions, watched and switched off. Agents do not make identity a new market. They make the existing one much bigger.
2. Identity is not one product. **Okta** (OKTA) mostly sells the check at the door (who are you?). **SailPoint** (SAIL) mostly sells the rulebook behind it (what are you allowed to do, and should you still be allowed?). They compete only at the edges.
3. Agents make the rulebook harder than the door. A login takes milliseconds. Deciding whether 10,000 unknown agents should hold access to payroll data is a governance problem. That favours SailPoint's layer. So does pricing: Okta charges per employee and gives agent sign-on away free, while SailPoint charges per identity it governs.
4. The market has done the opposite. Since the 10 April 2026 lows Okta is up about 250% and SailPoint about 91% (to the 8 October close). Okta now trades at a higher sales multiple than SailPoint despite growing at less than half the rate.
5. Okta's 2022 and 2023 breaches were priced, through a multi-year de-rating and net retention falling from 124% to 107%. They are not priced now. The 2026 re-rating rests on agent revenue that management says is "too small to show up in the numbers".
6. SailPoint's problems are different: a private-equity owner holding 84.6% of the shares, stock-based pay above free cash flow, and near-term growth slowing. These are entry-price problems, not thesis problems.

**Our view:** within listed identity, SailPoint is the better-structured way to own the agent thesis. The price to pay for it will be set by Thoma Bravo's eventual selling, not by the business.

## 1. What "identity security" actually is

![The identity stack: who logs in versus who governs](/img/sail-okta_chart0_identity_stack.png)

Think of a company as an airport.

- **Access management: Okta (OKTA), Microsoft (MSFT) Entra, Ping.** Passport control. You show a passport (password plus a second factor) and get a boarding pass (a digital token) that every gate accepts. This is single sign-on (SSO) and multi-factor authentication (MFA).
- **Identity governance, or IGA: SailPoint (SAIL), Saviynt, Microsoft Entra ID Governance.** The visa office. It decides who may enter which countries, for how long, and cancels the visa when you change jobs or leave. In practice it creates and removes accounts in hundreds of applications and produces the evidence auditors ask for.
- **Privileged access management, or PAM: CyberArk, now inside Palo Alto Networks (PANW), plus BeyondTrust and Delinea.** The vault holding the master keys. It controls the few accounts that can change everything.
- **Machine identity and secrets (CyberArk/Venafi, HashiCorp Vault, startups).** Keys, certificates and service accounts that software uses to talk to other software.
- **Identity threat detection and response, or ITDR: CrowdStrike (CRWD), Microsoft, Silverfort.** The security cameras. They spot a stolen boarding pass in use.
- **Identity for AI agents (everyone, all at once).** A passport, visa and kill switch for software that acts on its own.

The simplest split for investors: **authentication answers "who are you?" Governance answers "what should you be able to do, and who approved it?"** Okta's centre of gravity is the first question. SailPoint's is the second.

![SAIL and OKTA share prices since the April 2026 low](/img/sail-okta_chart1_price_since_april_low.png)

## 2. Why agents change the size of the problem

Before agents, identity mostly tracked employees, contractors and customers. Each person has roughly one identity, and headcount moves slowly. Agents break that in three ways.

**There are far more of them.** All of these ratios come from vendors, so read them as direction, not measurement:

- CyberArk's 2025 survey of 2,600 security leaders counted [82 machine identities per human](https://www.silicon.co.uk/press-release/machine-identities-outnumber-humans-by-more-than-80-to-1-new-report-exposes-the-exponential-threats-of-fragmented-identity-security).
- Entro, now owned by SailPoint (SAIL), measured 144 to 1 in H1 2025.
- SailPoint's CTO talked about ratios of 1 to 1,000 at its 2026 Investor Day.
- In one Fortune 500 trial in 2026, SailPoint found **more than 10,000 agents nobody knew existed** ([Q2 FY27 call](https://web.quartr.com/companies/20182?companyId=20182&documentId=4144542&documentType=transcript&eventId=688248&targetTime=343.64)).

**They hold real permissions.** An agent that books travel, reconciles invoices or answers HR queries is logged in with credentials. A compromised agent does not need to break in. It is already inside.

**Recent breaches were identity breaches, not code breaches:**

- **2024, Snowflake (SNOW) customers.** About [165 organisations](https://thehackernews.com/2024/06/snowflake-breach-exposes-165-customers.html) hit with stolen passwords on accounts without MFA.
- **Aug 2025, Salesloft Drift.** Stolen OAuth tokens (machine credentials) used to export Salesforce data from [more than 700 organisations](https://cyberscoop.com/salesforce-salesloft-drift-attack-spree-google/), including Cloudflare (NET) and Palo Alto Networks (PANW).
- **Apr 2025, Marks & Spencer (MKS).** Help-desk social engineering, with a profit hit guided at around £300m.
- **Jan 2026, ShinyHunters.** [Voice phishing](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/shinyhunters-claim-to-be-behind-sso-account-data-theft-attacks) against Okta (OKTA), Entra and Google sign-in, capturing MFA codes live.

The pattern is tokens, service accounts and phished sessions. Nobody broke the encryption. That is the demand case for identity in one line.

**The honest caveat: the money is still small.** Okta says its agent product is "too small to show up in the numbers". SailPoint reports "AI-driven ARR" above $70m, but that figure counts the whole contract value of any deal that includes an agentic product, human seats included. It is inflated by design. Agent identity today is a pipeline story, not a revenue story.

### More logins does not mean more revenue

The intuitive read is that Okta gains most from agents. Authentication volume is what explodes: every agent task can mean several token requests, so 10x to 100x more sign-ins and token grants is plausible. Governance volume grows too, but more slowly.

That is right about volume and wrong about money, because of how each company charges.

- **Okta is not paid per sign-in.**
  - Workforce identity is priced per employee per year.
  - Customer identity (Auth0) is priced per monthly active user, not per login.
  - Agent single sign-on is free in all Okta products.
  - More volume therefore mostly means more computing cost for Okta, not more revenue. That changes only if it moves to per-agent pricing, which management says it wants to do but has not done.
- **Login volume is also the easiest part to commoditise.** Microsoft Entra, AWS AgentCore, Google and, since September, CrowdStrike all issue agent tokens.
- **Governance is priced on the stock of identities, not the flow of logins.** Every agent is a new identity that needs an owner, a scope, a quarterly review and a kill switch. SailPoint sells capacity packs for non-human identities on top of human seats.

An analogy: Okta runs the toll booths but charges each car an annual pass, and rivals are handing out free passes to robot cars. SailPoint runs the vehicle registry. Every new robot car has to be registered, insured and inspected each year, and it pays for that.

Agents multiply both the flow (logins) and the stock (identities). Today only the stock gets paid for. That is the single most important point in this piece, and the main reason we prefer SailPoint's layer.

Okta's CEO confirmed the pricing point on the Q2 FY27 call: "Our pricing model is per user. If you want to buy Okta for AI agents, it's an uplift to your per user charge" ([call](https://web.quartr.com/companies/3870?companyId=3870&documentId=4081356&documentType=transcript&eventId=682009&targetTime=2964)).

He also showed where this could change. Agent single sign-on is now in Okta's base product with a usage cap that is "not going to \[be enforced\] right away", but "we're putting the framework and the scaffolding in there to have a consumption-based pricing eventually", because "agents are going to log in way more than people" ([call](https://web.quartr.com/companies/3870?companyId=3870&documentId=4081356&documentType=transcript&eventId=682009&targetTime=3055)).

So the flow-versus-stock argument holds today but is not permanent. If Okta starts charging for agent login volume, the bigger volume growth becomes its revenue growth. That is the single most important thing to watch at Okta.

### A tale of two breaches

The market still mostly prices cyber risk as broken code. The attacks that now do the damage use valid keys. Two stories show the difference. The company is fictional. Both attack methods are real.

**Story one: the code breach**

Meridian Logistics runs a file-transfer server so customers can send it shipping documents. One morning in 2023 a criminal group sends the server a carefully malformed request. A flaw in the software's code makes the server treat part of that request as a database command.

The attackers use this to plant a small program on the server, a "web shell", which lets them come back at will. They download every file on it.

This is how the [MOVEit Transfer attacks](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a) of May 2023 worked.

- **The fix:** a software patch.
- **The defences that matter:** vulnerability scanners, patching speed and network firewalls.
- **What the attacker needed:** a mistake in someone's code.

**Story two: the identity breach**

Two years earlier, Meridian's sales team added a chatbot to its website and connected it to Salesforce so chat leads flow into the CRM. An administrator clicked "Allow". Behind that click, Salesforce issued the chatbot vendor a token: a digital valet key that lets the vendor's software act inside Meridian's Salesforce without anyone logging in.

The key was never set to expire. It was granted "full" access, because that was the default. It sits in the vendor's cloud, alongside the keys of 700 other customers.

What happened next, in the [Salesloft Drift attack of August 2025](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift):

1. **March 2025.** Attackers take over the chatbot vendor's GitHub account. Meridian has no way to see it.
2. **The next three months.** The attackers explore quietly and reach the vendor's cloud account, where the customers' tokens are stored. They copy them.
3. **8 August.** They present Meridian's token to Salesforce. Salesforce sees a valid key from an approved app. There is no password prompt and no MFA challenge, because the token is proof that the login already happened. Nothing alerts.
4. **The next few days.** They count Meridian's records, then export every support case in one bulk job. At [Cloudflare, a real victim](https://blog.cloudflare.com/response-to-salesloft-drift-incident/), that export took about three minutes. Then they delete the job to cover their tracks.
5. **The real prize.** Support cases are full of text customers and engineers pasted in to fix problems: passwords, cloud access keys, API tokens. The attackers search for strings that look like AWS keys or Snowflake logins. Cloudflare found 104 of its own API tokens in its stolen cases. Each one is a new key to a new door.
6. **20 August.** Salesforce and the vendor revoke every chatbot token. Meridian learns from an advisory that it was breached twelve days earlier.

Google's threat team counted [more than 700 potentially affected organisations](https://cyberscoop.com/salesforce-salesloft-drift-attack-spree-google/).

**Why a stolen token is so harmful:**

- **It skips the front door.** MFA protects logins, and a token is what you get after logging in.
- **It belongs to a machine, so nobody notices it working at 3am.** No human is checking that it should not be exporting the whole database.
- **It is often over-scoped and never expires,** because whoever clicked "Allow" never had to choose otherwise.
- **It lives with a third party** whose security you cannot see.
- **It leads to more keys,** so one stolen token turns into a chain.

**What would have stopped it.** Not a patch, because there was no bug. What would have helped:

- An **inventory** of every connected app and token, each with a named human owner.
- **Least-privilege scopes and expiry dates.**
- **A quarterly review** that asks whether the chatbot still needs this.
- **Detection** of a machine identity suddenly doing a bulk export.

That is governance plus identity threat detection.

Every AI agent a company deploys is another chatbot integration: a non-human identity holding tokens to real systems. Companies are about to create these by the thousand. That is why we think the market has not caught up with where the risk now sits.

**What an individual can do.** There is no consumer version of a corporate security team watching your laptop, but you can get most of the way:

- **Built into macOS:** turn on automatic updates, FileVault and the firewall (it is off by default). Gatekeeper and XProtect run automatically ([Apple](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/protecting-against-malware-sec469d47bd8/web)).
- **Free tools from [Objective-See](https://objective-see.org/tools.html):** KnockKnock and BlockBlock show what installs itself to run at startup, and LuLu shows what phones out.
- **Paid scanners:** Bitdefender ($24.99 first year), Malwarebytes ($59.99 a year for 3 devices), or CrowdStrike Falcon Go ($59.99 per device a year, aimed at small businesses).
- **The single best upgrade is two hardware keys on your important accounts** (Apple requires at least two). They are the one control that defeats the real-time MFA phishing used against Okta, Entra and Google sign-ins in early 2026.

## 3. How big is the market?

The market that actually pays today is about $23bn, growing about 12% a year. The company TAM figures are four times that.

| Measure | Figure | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IAM spending, 2025 | $20.7bn | Gartner 1Q26 outlook |
| IAM spending, 2026E | $23.4bn (+11.8%) | Gartner 1Q26 outlook |
| IAM spending, 2030E | $30.9bn | Gartner 1Q26 outlook |
| Okta TAM claim | $80bn ($50bn workforce + $30bn customer) | [Okta deck](https://web.quartr.com/companies/3870?companyId=3870&documentId=4078517&documentType=slide&eventId=682009&sp=31) |
| SailPoint TAM claim | $90bn (was $10bn in 2017) | [SailPoint Investor Day](https://web.quartr.com/companies/20182?companyId=20182&documentId=3599477&documentType=slide&eventId=669261&sp=8) |

In text: Gartner puts identity and access management spending at $20.7bn in 2025, $23.4bn in 2026 (up 11.8%) and $30.9bn in 2030. Okta claims an $80bn market ($50bn workforce, $30bn customer). SailPoint claims $90bn, up from $10bn in 2017.

The CEO of Okta (OKTA) said it himself on the Q4 FY26 call: identity is ["roughly $20 billion TAM right now in terms of what people spend"](https://web.quartr.com/companies/3870?companyId=3870&documentId=3313013&documentType=transcript&eventId=409956&targetTime=1958.56). The $80bn and $90bn figures assume every company buys every product. They are ambitions, not markets.

Other reference points:

- **Access management alone** was $5.85bn in 2023, growing 17.6% ([Gartner via ISMG](https://www.bankinfosecurity.net/microsoft-ping-okta-dominate-access-management-gartner-mq-a-27214)).
- **SailPoint** (SAIL) claims 23.2% of identity governance. Okta puts Microsoft (MSFT) at about 40% of workforce access management and itself at about 30%. Both are company claims.
- **The agent layer is the option on top.** If agents are priced like people, today's $23bn is too small. If agents are a cheap add-on (Okta already gives agent single sign-on away free), the market grows but the price per identity collapses.

The number to watch is not the TAM. It is whether either company starts charging per agent rather than per employee, and at what price.

## 4. How identity plugs into the rest of the stack

Identity is the reference point every other security layer checks against. Here is one request, step by step, when an employee or an agent opens a business application.

1. **The device.** The CrowdStrike (CRWD) agent on the laptop reports whether the device is healthy.
2. **The gate.** A zero-trust gateway from Zscaler (ZS), Cloudflare (NET) or Netskope intercepts the request and redirects it to the identity provider.
3. **The passport check.** Okta (OKTA) or Microsoft (MSFT) Entra checks the password and second factor and issues a signed token (SAML or OIDC, the two standard formats).
4. **The decision.** The gateway combines "who is this" from Okta with "is the device clean" from CrowdStrike, then lets the request through or blocks it.
5. **The application.** Salesforce, Workday or SAP accepts the token. The account and its permissions inside that app were created in advance by the governance system, here SailPoint (SAIL), over a standard called SCIM.
6. **The watch.** Risk signals flow both ways over the Shared Signals Framework. If CrowdStrike sees malware, it can tell Okta to kill the session and tell SailPoint to strip the access, mid-session.

**On Cloudflare specifically:** the CDN is not the link. The link is Cloudflare's zero-trust product (Cloudflare One / Access), which works with [any identity provider](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/integrations/identity-providers/) and consumes the token Okta or Entra issues. Today Cloudflare and Zscaler are partners of the identity vendors, not competitors. They are the bouncer. The identity provider is the guest list.

**Why both a gateway and an identity provider?** They answer different questions, and neither can answer the other's.

- **The identity provider (Okta, Entra) is the authority on who you are.** It is connected to HR, holds your password and second factor, and knows your groups. A company has one.
- **The gateway (Zscaler, Cloudflare, Netskope) is the enforcement point on the path.** Every request passes through it, and it sees the destination, device, location and content. But it does not know who you are unless someone it trusts tells it.

Office analogy:

- HR issues your staff badge (Okta).
- The guard at each door checks the badge is genuine and not expired, checks your bag, and checks this door is on your list (the gateway).
- The facilities office decides which doors your badge should open, and removes doors when you change role (SailPoint).

**What is the token?** It is not a bare yes or no. It is a signed digital note, roughly: *issued by okta.com, user alex@company, groups investment and finance, signed in with a hardware key at 10:02, valid until 11:02.*

- Okta signs it with its private key. Cloudflare checks the signature with Okta's public key, like checking the watermark on a banknote, so it does not need to call Okta on every request.
- "Works with any identity provider" means Cloudflare accepts badges from Okta, Entra, Google and others.

**How does the gateway decide?** It combines four signals, then allows, blocks or asks for more proof (a fresh hardware-key tap, say):

1. Who: the token.
2. Which device: health reported by the endpoint agent (CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender), such as encrypted, patched, no malware alert.
3. Context: location, time, network, unusual behaviour.
4. What: the app requested and, for some traffic, the content (malware coming in, client files going out).

"Zero trust" means no request is trusted just because it comes from inside the office network. Every request is checked, every time.

**What changes with agents.** The agent gets its own identity, registered as acting for a named person. When it calls a tool (Slack, Jira, a database), the identity provider issues a short-lived token scoped to that one task. In July 2026 the Model Context Protocol, the standard most agents use to call tools, made [Enterprise-Managed Authorization](https://infoq.com/news/2026/07/mcp-ema-enterprise-auth/) stable. It uses Okta's Cross App Access design, Okta is the first supported identity provider, and Anthropic has adopted it across Claude. That is a real standards win for Okta at the door.

The governance question sits one level up: *should this person be allowed to hand this access to an agent at all, and who reviews that every quarter?* That is the visa office, and it is SailPoint's layer.

**Partner or competitor? It is shifting:**

- **CrowdStrike** feeds signals into both Okta and SailPoint. On 2 September 2026 it also launched its own [Agentic Identity Provider](https://secure.businesswire.com/news/home/20260902817711/en/Introducing-the-CrowdStrike-Agentic-Identity-Provider-the-Foundation-for-AI-Agent-Identity-Security), a direct move into Okta's layer.
- **Palo Alto** closed its \~$25bn [CyberArk acquisition](https://paloaltonetworks.com/company/press/2026/palo-alto-networks-completes-acquisition-of-cyberark-to-secure-the-ai-era) in February 2026. It now owns privileged access and machine identity.
- **Cisco** bought [Astrix](https://blogs.cisco.com/news/cisco-announces-intent-to-acquire-astrix-security) (agent and machine identity, closed June 2026) to add to Duo.
- **AWS** is a partner. It named SailPoint its [preferred identity governance solution for agentic AI](https://www.sailpoint.com/press-releases/sailpoint-aws-agentic-ai-strategic-collaboration-agreement) on AWS (March 2026).

The pattern so far: the platforms are mostly moving into Okta's layer. SailPoint's layer is safer, but not safe.

| Who | Moving into | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CrowdStrike | Okta's layer | Agentic Identity Provider (Sep 2026), SGNL authorisation (Jan 2026) |
| Cisco | Okta's layer and machine identity | Duo plus Astrix (Jun 2026) |
| Microsoft | Both layers | Entra in E3/E5, ID Governance add-on, Agent ID |
| Palo Alto | Privileged and machine identity, some governance | CyberArk, which had bought Zilla (governance, $165m) |
| ServiceNow | SailPoint's layer | Veza access-governance graph (>$1bn reported) |
| Okta | SailPoint's layer | Okta Identity Governance, its largest new product |
| Saviynt | SailPoint's layer | $700m of fresh capital (Dec 2025) |

In text: CrowdStrike (CRWD) is moving into Okta's layer with its Agentic Identity Provider (September 2026) and SGNL authorisation (January 2026). Cisco (CSCO) is moving into Okta's layer and machine identity with Duo plus Astrix (June 2026). Microsoft (MSFT) is in both layers through Entra, ID Governance and Agent ID. Palo Alto Networks (PANW) owns privileged and machine identity, plus some governance, through CyberArk. ServiceNow (NOW) is moving into SailPoint's layer with Veza. Okta is moving into SailPoint's layer with Okta Identity Governance. Saviynt raised $700m in December 2025.

SailPoint says Microsoft is "a non-factor in enterprise IGA" and that it has "never lost a deal" to Zilla. These are company claims, and we found no documented losses either way. The one to watch is **ServiceNow**, because it already runs the IT workflows where access requests start.

**Okta is the clearest threat to SailPoint, and its Q2 deck says so.** Okta for AI Agents now includes "agent governance and access certification with Okta Identity Governance". Okta calls itself the "first independent neutral identity platform to bring AI agent governance" to market. Governance is the largest of its new products.

The pitch is consolidation. McKinnon described a Fortune 25 customer with "200 identity vendors" that "could save tens of millions of dollars by standardizing on us" ([call](https://web.quartr.com/companies/3870?companyId=3870&documentId=4081356&documentType=transcript&eventId=682009&targetTime=1691)). He also argues agent security should start from the login layer, not specialist tools: "It makes sense to start it from the broad IdP" ([call](https://web.quartr.com/companies/3870?companyId=3870&documentId=4081356&documentType=transcript&eventId=682009&targetTime=3237)).

SailPoint argues the opposite: governance is the hard part, and a login vendor's governance is "below the line". Neither company discloses win rates against the other. Okta's governance growth and SailPoint's net new ARR, side by side each quarter, are the scoreboard.

## 5. Who else is in the market

Only three listed pure plays remain: Okta (OKTA), SailPoint (SAIL) and Yubico (YUBICO on Nasdaq Stockholm, hardware security keys). CyberArk disappeared into Palo Alto in February 2026. Everyone else is a platform with an identity division, or private.

**Platforms with identity exposure**

- **Microsoft (MSFT) Entra.** The largest vendor by users. Entra ID P1 comes in Microsoft 365 E3 and P2 in E5. [Entra ID Governance](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/microsoft-entra-pricing) is $7 per user per month and Entra Suite $12. [Entra Agent ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/whats-new-agent-id) is generally available, and Agent 365 launched at $15 per user in May 2026. No revenue disclosed.
- **Palo Alto Networks (PANW) / CyberArk (rebranded Idira).** FY26 pro forma revenue $1.26bn, +21%.
- **CrowdStrike (CRWD).** Identity ARR $585m, +34%, after buying SGNL ($740m) and Seraphic (\~$400m) in January 2026.
- **Cisco (CSCO).** Duo plus Astrix.
- **IBM.** HashiCorp Vault ($6.4bn, 2025), and a leader in Gartner's access management ranking.
- **Others moving in:** Twilio (Stytch, customer identity), ServiceNow ([Veza](https://www.securityweek.com/servicenow-to-acquire-identity-security-firm-veza-in-reported-1-billion-deal/amp/), >$1bn reported), Snowflake ([Natoma](https://investors.snowflake.com/news/news-details/2026/Snowflake-Announces-Intent-to-Acquire-Natoma-Providing-Secure-Connectivity-For-The-Agentic-Enterprise/default.aspx), agent tool governance).

**Private companies**

| Company | What it does | Latest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Saviynt | Governance, SailPoint's main rival | [$700m at \~$3bn](https://www.barchart.com/story/news/36524676/saviynt-raises-700m-at-approximately-3b-valuation-in-kkr-led-round-to-establish-identity-security-as-the-foundation-for-the-ai-era), KKR, Dec 2025 |
| Ping Identity | Access management, merged with ForgeRock | Owned by Thoma Bravo |
| Silverfort | Threat detection, MFA everywhere | $116m Series D, 2024 |
| Persona | Identity verification | $200m at $2bn, 2025 |
| ID.me | Consumer identity verification | $340m at >$2bn, 2025 |
| ConductorOne | AI-native governance | $79m Series B, Oct 2025 |
| Keycard | Agent identity | $38m at launch, Oct 2025 |
| Clutch, Aembit | Machine identity | Series A |

In text: Saviynt raised $700m at about $3bn, led by KKR, in December 2025. Ping Identity is owned by Thoma Bravo. Silverfort raised a $116m Series D in 2024. Persona raised $200m at $2bn and ID.me $340m at over $2bn, both in 2025. ConductorOne raised a $79m Series B and Keycard $38m at launch, both in October 2025. Clutch and Aembit are at Series A.

**The 2025-26 deal pattern matters more than any single name.** The platforms bought the agent and machine-identity startups rather than build them:

- Astrix → Cisco
- Entro → SailPoint ($122.6m per its 10-Q, not the \~$200m reported in the press)
- Oasis → Cyera (\~$1bn)
- [Permiso → Okta](https://www.okta.com/newsroom/press-releases/okta-signs-definitive-agreement-to-acquire-permiso-security/)
- Natoma → Snowflake
- Veza → ServiceNow
- SGNL → CrowdStrike
- Zilla and Venafi → CyberArk, then CyberArk → Palo Alto

This is the strongest evidence that identity is a control point worth owning. It is also a warning that competition for the agent layer will be fierce.

**One thing worth noticing:** Thoma Bravo owns SailPoint (84.6%), Ping Identity and Imprivata. In December 2024 SailPoint bought Imprivata's governance business from its own parent for $16.4m. The same sponsor sits across both access management and governance.

### The third pure play: Yubico

Yubico makes YubiKeys: small USB or NFC hardware keys that prove a real person is present at login. A fake website cannot trick the key into signing for it, which makes them the most phishing-resistant login method available. After Google gave 85,000+ staff security keys in 2017, it reported no successful account phishing ([Krebs](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2018/07/google-security-keys-neutralized-employee-phishing/)).

- **Listing:** Nasdaq Stockholm, via a September 2023 SPAC merger. Founded by Stina and Jakob Ehrensvärd.
- **Customers:** 4,500+ businesses, including 19 of the 20 largest US tech companies. Public sector and defence is the largest one-off buyer.
- **FY2025:** sales SEK 2,218m (-4.7%, +1.4% excluding currency), EBIT margin 9.0%.
- **Q2 2026:** sales SEK 544m (+9.0%), EBIT margin 14.4%, gross margin 80.1%.
- **Weak spots:**
  - Bookings -7.2%, the third straight fall.
  - ARR growth slowed to 4.4%.
  - A leak-driven profit warning in March 2026.
  - An acting CEO since December 2025.

Sources: [FY25 report](https://investors.yubico.com/en/year-end-report-january-december-2025/), [Q2-26 deck](https://investors.yubico.com/en/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/03/Presentation-Interim-Report-Q2-2026.pdf).

**The OpenAI link:**

- **April 2026:** OpenAI and Yubico announced a "strategic, long-term partnership". Co-branded keys are sold to ChatGPT users through OpenAI's Advanced Account Security programme ([Yubico](https://www.yubico.com/press-releases/openai-and-yubico-partner-to-bring-custom-phishing-resistant-yubikeys-to-openai-users/)).
- **1 September 2026:** OpenAI made hardware-backed passkeys mandatory for its Trusted Access for Cyber program, the tier with its most capable cyber models ([Forrester](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/openai-makes-hardware-passkeys-mandatory-for-its-highest-end-cyber-model/)).
- **No terms are disclosed:** no volumes, revenue share or pricing.

This is the first sign of frontier labs mandating hardware keys for their most dangerous tools.

- **Bear case:** passkeys stored on phones do much of the same job for free, and revenue is mostly one-off hardware.
- **What to watch:** whether the OpenAI deal shows up in bookings. The Q3 report is due on 5 November and the Capital Markets Day on 19 November 2026.

## 6. SailPoint: the rulebook

SailPoint (SAIL) has sold one thing since 2005: identity governance. ARR is $1.23bn, growing 25%, and the business is moving from on-premise licences to cloud.

### What it sells

- **Identity Security Cloud** on a shared data layer called Atlas. This is the cloud product.
- **Add-on modules:** machine identities, agent identities, contractors and other non-employees, data access, cloud permissions and access risk.
- **Agentic Fabric (2026):** governance for agent identities, sold standalone even to non-SailPoint customers.
- **IdentityIQ:** the legacy on-premise product. Moving these customers to the cloud is the biggest growth driver.
- **What it will not do:** management says it will not build traditional privileged access management.

### How it works, day to day

SailPoint does not write one rulebook for everyone. Each customer writes its own rules, and SailPoint provides the machinery to enforce them and prove it. Think of it as the accounting system for access: every company has its own chart of accounts, but the ledger software is shared.

1. **Connect.** Read who has what in every system: SAP, Workday, Salesforce, AWS, mainframes.
2. **Model.** Define roles and policies. A classic one: nobody may both create a supplier and approve payments to it. That is a SOX control.
3. **Run the lifecycle.** Joiners get access on day one. Movers lose old access when they change team. Leavers lose everything on their last day.
4. **Certify.** Each quarter managers confirm or revoke their staff's access. This is the evidence auditors ask for.
5. **Recommend.** The cloud product learns patterns across about 3,300 customers and flags outliers.

For agents the same machinery applies. Discover every agent, assign an accountable human owner ("that agent will not be able to alter its own ownership", says McClain), give it the least access it needs, review it like an employee, and switch it off when it misbehaves.

SailPoint does not keep bad bots out at the gate. That is Okta's and the gateway's job. SailPoint decides who is on the guest list, with which keys, and who signs for them.

### Revenue mix, Q2 FY27 (quarter to 31-Jul-26)

| Line | $m | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SaaS (cloud) | 193.9 | 63% |
| Term licences (on-premise) | 56.2 | 18% |
| Maintenance (legacy) | 35.5 | 11% |
| Other subscription | 9.7 | 3% |
| Services | 13.6 | 4% |
| **Total** | **308.8** |  |

In text: SailPoint's Q2 FY27 revenue (quarter to 31 July 2026) was $308.8m. SaaS was $193.9m (63%), term licences $56.2m (18%), maintenance $35.5m (11%), other subscription $9.7m (3%) and services $13.6m (4%).

Source: [Q2 FY27 earnings release](https://web.quartr.com/companies/20182?companyId=20182&documentId=3695764&documentType=report&eventId=688248). No revenue is disclosed by module. What is disclosed:

- "Emerging" modules were 17% of net new ARR in Q4 FY26 and 20% in Q1 FY27.
- AI-driven products were above 30% of net new ARR in Q2 FY27.
- Customers who adopt them raise annual spend by more than 60%.

**Are "emerging modules" the agent business?** Largely, yes.

- **Q4 FY26:** management said "a significant portion" came from AI identity, specifically Agent Identity Security, Machine Identity Security and Data Access Security ([call](https://web.quartr.com/companies/20182?companyId=20182&documentId=3787275&documentType=transcript&eventId=418901&targetTime=1586.72)).
- **Q1 FY27:** about a third of cloud migrations pulled them in, "typically… those related to agentic".
- **From Q2 the metric changed** to "AI-driven ARR". It counts whole contracts that include agentic products, and even suite customers with "an immediate upgrade path". The definition is generous, and management will not split human from agent revenue.

### The numbers
